summaries.example: Imagine a dragon. There is no real dragon in front of you, but your thought is still about a dragon. Ancient philosophers asked how a thought can be about something that may not exist. They also asked how someone can believe something false, such as thinking a toy is a real animal.
summaries.summary: Intentionality is the “aboutness” of mental life. A belief is about something, a wish reaches toward something, and a memory concerns something. The ancient Greeks explored difficult cases: we can imagine nonexistent things, believe something false, and think about one thing under a particular description. Parmenides argued that thought and speech cannot concern what is not. Some later thinkers accepted this idea and limited what thought can be about; others used it to argue that whatever we can think about must exist. Plato examined these puzzles, especially false belief, and eventually explained error as a mismatch between parts of a statement. Aristotle said that mental representations can help explain thoughts about absent or imaginary things. The Stoics offered several accounts, including objects that exist only in thought and meanings expressed by language. The entry also explains why following the history of a concept is more useful than simply following the history of a word.
key_ideas: Intentionality means that minds can be about things, including things that are absent or imaginary.
Parmenides and other early Greek thinkers wondered whether we can think about what does not exist.
Plato tried to explain how false thoughts and false statements are possible.
Aristotle used inner representations, while Stoic philosophers proposed different kinds of objects or contents for thought.
Ancient philosophers did not all use the same words, so historians study their ideas, not just their vocabulary.
summaries.why_it_matters: These ancient debates help us understand how thinking works. They connect everyday questions—such as imagining a monster, remembering a friend, or making a mistake—to bigger questions about minds, language, truth, and reality. They also show that philosophers can use different explanations for the same puzzling experience.

important_terms.definition: The feature of a thought, feeling, wish, or belief that makes it about something.
What a thought, belief, or feeling is about.
A mistake in thinking or speaking, such as believing that one thing is another.
A mental picture or trace that helps the mind think about something, according to Aristotle.

questions_to_think_about: Can you think about something that does not exist?
How can someone make a mistake if their thought is about something?
Is an imaginary object the same as a real object?
Which explanation seems most helpful: an inner picture, an object of thought, or a meaning?

summaries.example: Suppose a student thinks that the Morning Star is visible at dawn but that Venus is not, without realizing that the two names refer to the same object. The student’s thoughts concern the same thing, yet the descriptions guide thought differently. This illustrates that intentionality involves not only what a thought is about, but also how its content presents that object. A different problem arises when the student imagines a nonexistent planet: the thought seems directed toward something even though no such planet exists.
summaries.summary: The entry presents intentionality as the problem of explaining the aboutness or content of mental states. It warns that the history of the term is not the same as the history of the problem: ancient philosophers may address intentionality without using later technical vocabulary, and the same vocabulary can express different theories. The central difficulty concerns cases in which thought seems directed at what is absent, nonexistent, or not the case, as well as cases in which one object is considered under different aspects. A direct-relational model appears attractive, but it conflicts with the claim that relations require existing relata when we imagine fictional objects or think falsely. Parmenides, Protagoras, and Gorgias represent different responses to this conflict. Plato examines false belief and speech, eventually distinguishing a subject from what is said of it, so that falsehood can result from an incorrect combination. Aristotle appeals to phantasmata—bodily or perceptual representations—that can support thought even without the external object. The Stoics divide their responses: early Stoics posit non-existent or merely thought objects, while Chrysippus emphasizes lekta, incorporeal semantic contents. The source also traces related ideas through Stoic theories of vision and Augustine, while stressing that later terminology should not control interpretation of the ancient theories.
key_ideas: A history of intentionality should track philosophical problems and competing conceptions, not merely words such as intention.
A central puzzle arises from the tension between three claims: thought is a direct relation, relations require existing relata, and we can think about nonexistent things.
Parmenides is read as denying thought or speech about what is not; Protagoras and Gorgias develop sharply different responses to this pressure.
Plato preserves the relational character of thought while analyzing falsehood through error, representation, and finally the structure of statements.
Aristotle explains many cases through bodily changes or phantasmata, while recognizing that perception and thought are not the whole of intentional life.
Early Stoics allow objects of thought that do not exist, whereas Chrysippus explains content through lekta, abstract “sayables” that can be true or false.
summaries.why_it_matters: Intentionality lies at the intersection of philosophy of mind, language, logic, and metaphysics. Understanding the ancient arguments clarifies why it is difficult to explain error, imagination, reference, and thought about nonexistent things. The competing solutions also reveal different assumptions about whether mental states relate directly to objects, depend on representations, or have abstract contents.

important_terms.definition: The feature of mental states—such as belief, desire, perception, and thought—in virtue of which they are about or represent something.
What a mental state presents, asserts, or otherwise has as its meaning; content may be true or false.
The philosophical difficulty of explaining how a mental state can concern something absent, nonexistent, false, or presented under one aspect rather than another.
A model in which thought is directly related to the thing thought about; this creates pressure when the object does not exist.
An internal state or structure that stands between a thinker and the external thing, helping explain thought about absent or nonexistent objects.
Plato’s account in the Sophist that a false statement combines a subject with a predicate that does not correctly apply to it.
Aristotle’s term for perceptual traces or images that support imagination, thought, memory, desire, and action.
A Stoic abstract item signified by language and functioning as the content of a representation or statement.

questions_to_think_about: Which part of the inconsistent triad should be rejected: direct relation, the need for existing relata, or thought about nonexistent things?
Does Plato’s subject-predicate account explain every kind of false thought, or mainly false statements of a certain structure?
Why might an internal representation be useful for explaining dreams, hopes, or thoughts about extinct individuals?
Are the Stoic ennoēmata and lekta objects of thought, contents of thought, or different kinds of entities?
Can a mental state have content without the thinker possessing the concepts needed to describe it in words?

summaries.example: You picture a unicorn while writing a story. Your picture and your thoughts are clearly about a unicorn, even though there is no real unicorn in the room. Now imagine that you mistake a bicycle for a horse. Your belief is about something real, but it is false. Ancient philosophers used puzzles like these to ask what makes a thought have a subject and how mistakes are possible.
summaries.summary: Intentionality is the fact that thoughts, beliefs, desires, perceptions, and other mental states are about something. The ancient philosophers discussed this issue through questions about falsehood, imagination, and nonexistent things. Parmenides argued that what is not cannot be thought or spoken about. His claim could be used in different ways: some thinkers used it to deny error, while Gorgias used examples of impossible things to challenge the connection between thought and reality. Plato kept returning to the puzzle of false belief. In the Sophist, he suggested that a statement has a subject and something said about that subject, so a statement can be meaningful but false when its parts do not fit the facts. Aristotle explained thought about absent or fictional things with phantasmata, internal traces that can represent things without being those things. The Stoics took another route. Early Stoics allowed thought to be directed at things that do not exist, while Chrysippus focused on lekta, abstract meanings that serve as the contents of statements and representations. The entry argues that this history should follow changing problems and theories rather than assuming that one modern definition is the goal toward which all ancient philosophy was moving.
key_ideas: The ancient discussion is about a philosophical problem, not just about finding an early use of a particular word.
Parmenides questioned whether anyone can think or speak about what is not.
Protagoras and Gorgias responded differently: one route protects ordinary thought by treating what is thought as real, while another rejects the tight link between thought and reality.
Plato explored why false belief is difficult and later explained false statements through a mismatch between a subject and what is said about it.
Aristotle used representations to explain how thought can concern absent or imaginary things.
The Stoics offered two broad approaches: thought can have non-existent objects, or mental states can have abstract contents that language expresses.
summaries.why_it_matters: These debates show why simple explanations of thinking are not enough. A mind can remember what is gone, imagine what is fictional, believe what is false, and focus on one feature of something while ignoring others. Studying the ancient proposals helps us compare different ways of explaining meaning, mental representation, truth, and mistakes.

important_terms.definition: The way a mental state is directed toward or is about something, such as an object, event, idea, or imagined creature.
The meaning or information carried by a thought, belief, sentence, or other mental state.
The thing a thought or feeling is about; it may be absent, fictional, or nonexistent.
A belief or statement that does not match how things are.
The view that a thought is directly related to the thing it is about.
Something inside the thinker that represents an external thing or supports thought about it.
Aristotle’s name for perceptual traces or images used in imagination and thought.
The Stoic term for an abstract meaning or “sayable” expressed by words and sentences.

questions_to_think_about: If you can imagine a unicorn, does something have to exist for your thought to be about it?
Can a thought be false even when it is about a real thing?
Would an inner representation explain a dream better than a direct connection to an outside object?
What is the difference between the object of a thought and the content of that thought?
Why might historians study an ancient philosopher’s reasoning instead of looking only for modern technical terms?
